catalog_quote: [Rajasingh 2019 p. xvi, 2.1 Phonology] Length and stress are observed, but not as phonemic; and, they have a bearing in determining the root of words. [p. xvii, 2.2 Morphology] The word is constituted by either root alone (see, for example, hēng /xeˑŋ/ p88) or by root and affixes (see, for example, in-töön-ngö-lah /ʔint̪ɑˑnŋɑlɑx/ p74). All roots are monosyllabic, and they are tensed and stressed. The tenseness will be to a full length in the case of open syllables (see, for example, chukë /cukɛː/ p45) and to a half in the case of closed ones (see, for example, fal /fɑˑl/ p17). In the case of syllables whose nuclei are constituted by diphthongs the tenseness and stress are found to fall either on the first or on the second constituent of the nuclei. [Man 1889 p. 221, Rules] In dissyllabic words stress occurs on the second syllable unless there is a long vowel in the first syllable. ... In trisyllabic and polysyllabic words stress usually occurs on the penultimate syllable whenever neither or none of the other syllables have accented vowels. [Man 1889 p. xi] Unlike Chinese and Burmese, no instance has been discovered in any of the dialects in which the meaning of words depends on tone, accent, or emphasis, but, in common with many other tongues, sentences can be rendered affirmative or interrogative by change of tone or stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not lexically contrastive in any Nicobarese dialect. In Man's Nicobar-language orthography (rules formulated from Nancowry/Central and applied to the Southern column of his six-dialect comparative list), a disyllable is stressed on its final syllable unless the first syllable has a long vowel, in which case that long first syllable is stressed; longer words are stressed on the penult unless some other syllable carries a long ('accented') vowel, which then takes the stress. In practice this is stress on the root/main syllable, i.e. the syllable with the long vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Man for any dialect. (Sidwell 2018 p. 116 reports, for Nancowry only, a secondary stress in words of three or more syllables.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond 'usually' for tri-/polysyllables; in Appendix C several polysyllabic Southern forms carry no stress mark at all (e.g. pattai, ke-wet, ham-lare, penhon-wihla) although Man's convention says every polysyllable is marked.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms in a dictionary/wordlist; the sentence-level remark (interrogative by tone or stress) is phrase-level. The placement rule is a statement about the Nicobar language as a whole in Man's alphabet, exemplified from Nancowry; its bearing on Southern Nicobarese is only that the ~300 Southern items of Appendix C are transcribed with the same stress mark under the same rules. No source states stress placement for Southern Nicobarese specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: No primary phonological description of Southern Nicobarese (sout2689 / nik) exists: Glottolog lists zero descriptive references, and Sidwell 2018/2022 inventory only wordlists (de Roepstorff 1875, Man 1889 App. C, Radhakrishnan 1978, Nandan 1993, Rajasingh 2019). The quoted stress rule is Man's rule for writing 'the Nicobar language' generally, formulated and exemplified from Nancowry = Central Nicobarese (Glottolog cent1990, ISO ncb); Man's own Appendix C applies the same orthography and stress mark to the 'Southern: Coast inhabitants (about 290)' lect, i.e. the coastal Great Nicobar variety (Lo'ong / Takahanyilang; Sidwell 2022 finds Man's and Rajasingh's Great Nicobar lists ~20% lexically different, so Man's data may represent a lect distinct from the modern Tokahanilahngo). The p. xi 'no dialect has lexical tone/accent contrast' remark is explicitly pan-dialectal. Treat the placement rule as attributed to Southern Nicobarese only by extension; a catalog reviewer may prefer to file it as 'stress not contrastive; placement rule inherited from Central' rather than as a Southern-specific rule.
